title: Karma-Causing Events & Inputs — From Incident to Ledger
status: conversation archaeology + repository synthesis + recovery map
purpose: Reconstruct the events, statements, conflicts and perceived harms that fed Tim Dooley's later karma/spiritual-bank/debt model. The goal is to distinguish the triggering event, Tim's contemporaneous wording, later reinterpretation, symbolic residue and possible repair path instead of treating karmic debt as a free-floating number.
epistemic_rule: Project claims about karma, spiritual debt, Dogs, Mud, Swamp, rubble, trafficking, grooming, divine judgment or collective responsibility are not empirical findings by themselves. Every real-world event must keep its evidence class, named actors, date, source, allegation/finding distinction and counterevidence. Illness or later misfortune is never treated as proven karmic causation.

largest_new_observations: The trillion figure is downstream of a much older consequence grammar. The 2016 reciprocity/consequence language and later years of archive/pursuit themes predate explicit trillion-scale accounting.

The April 2025 Turning provides the conceptual bridge: invisible accumulated burden becomes visible relational topology. This helps explain why 2026 debt rapidly expands into maps, networks, infrastructure and obligations.

Positive karma and karmic debt are not clean opposites in the project. They can be counterpart entries: burden survived/held on Tim's side becomes stored capacity or claim while unresolved responsibility appears as debt on the other side.

The ledger increasingly moves from grievance to systems theory. By mid/late 2026 its strongest form is less 'someone owes Tim money' and more 'ordinary ledgers fail to price certain persistent social, reputational, institutional and human consequences.'

The archive needs a closure mechanism as much as an accumulation mechanism. Without correction, restitution, release or demonstrable non-liability, karmic accounting risks reproducing the same endless entanglement it criticizes.
The recurring metaphor of holding/carrying is central: the project repeatedly treats unresolved consequence as something stored until it can be named, transformed, repaired or released.
